newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communists on offensive against sick Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Communists on offensive against sick Yeltsin.

text.p: Russia's communists opened a new political barrage against ailing President Boris Yeltsin on Monday, calling on the president to quit and accusing the Kremlin of misleading the electorate.

Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, runner-up to Yeltsin in Russia's July presidential election, said a comment from a top doctor that Yeltsin probably had a heart attack during the campaign showed the Kremlin had deceived voters.
"(Concealing the heart attack) amounts to falsification. The elections were not fair," Zyuganov told Reuters at the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly in Strasbourg.

In Moscow, the communist speaker of the State Duma lower house of parliament said Yeltsin, 65, should step down if the surgeons refused to operate and told him he had to simply eke out his life by avoiding stress and overwork.
"The situation in Russia is such that (the president) cannot have an easy work schedule," Gennady Seleznyov told reporters.

Yeltsin said earlier this month he would have a heart operation at the end of September. But doctors have fought shy of setting a date for the planned surgery, which will improve the blood supply to the president's heart.

Top heart surgeon Renat Akchurin, who is expected to lead the operation, said this weekend that surgery might be delayed for six to eight weeks. There was a risk of the operation being cancelled altogether, he added.
Russian share prices fell over three percent on news of the likely delay.

"Controversial news about the date of Yeltsin's heart operation is very depressing for Western investors, and they were mainly sellers, not buyers, of shares today," said Yuri Agaronik of share traders Prospekt.
The communist campaign for Yeltsin to step down heightened the political uncertainty in Russia due to the president's ill-health.
The Kremlin retreated into silence and a spokesman said there may be no comment until a council of doctors, including foreign experts, meets on Wednesday to decide when or whether to operate.
U.S. bypass pioneer Michael DeBakey flew into Moscow to join the team on Monday, but he declined to comment on the planned operation because he had not had access to the medical facts.
DeBakey, who works in Houston and is 23 years older than his new patient, conducted the world's first successful heart bypass operation. "I'm always optimistic," he said.
Yeltsin dropped out of sight before the July 3 runoff vote and aides initially said he had a cold or had lost his voice.
Yeltsin broke the secrecy on September 5 by saying he would have surgery at the end of the month to avoid a "passive life".
Now he is in hospital and is under doctors' orders to take things even easier than in the summer, when he fished, shot ducks and hunted boar.
Russians and governments abroad are left guessing about who is running the nuclear-armed country, which still has a fragile grip on democracy five years after the Soviet Union fell apart.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who would take over to organise new elections if Yeltsin were to step down, has been given some extra duties and will take over full presidential powers for the few hours Yeltsin is on the operating table.
But that has not quashed speculation over who would take over permanently if Yeltsin were to step down nor the impression that top officials are already jostling for position.
"The longer the operation is put off, the more unstable the situation will be," said Lyudmila Telen of Moscow News weekly.
